### Part A - Creating Matrices
```{r}
# TODO: Create a 3x3 matrix called m1 containing the numbers 1 to 9,
# using matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
# Print m1

m1 <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
m1
```

```{r}
# TODO: Create a second 3x3 matrix called m2 with the SAME numbers 1:9,
# but this time add the argument byrow = TRUE
# Print m2 and compare it to m1

m2 <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
m2
```

```{r}
scores <- matrix(c(88, 92, 79, 95, 84, 90), nrow = 2, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
rownames(scores) <- c("Quiz1", "Quiz2")
colnames(scores) <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid")

# TODO: Print scores and confirm the row/column names were applied
scores
```

Question #1:

Compare m1 and m2 above. Both were built from 1:9 with nrow = 3, ncol = 3, but they look different.
Explain exactly what byrow = TRUE changes about how R fills a matrix.

The two are different because m1 arranges the datasets vertically from one column to another by default while m2 with the argument byrow = TRUE arranges the datasets horizontally from one row to another instead of columns. 

Question #2

If you tried matrix(1:8, nrow = 3, ncol = 3) (only 8 numbers for 9 slots), what do you think would happen?
Test it and explain the result, including any warning message.
```{r}
matrix(1:8, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
```

The result is the numbers from 1 to 8 arranged by columns with the last position being 1 because the values are recycled since the number of elements is not a multiple of the number of rows which is 3. The warning message shows: Warning in matrix(1:8, nrow = 3, ncol = 3): data length [8] is not a
sub-multiple or multiple of the number of rows [3].

### Part B - Subsetting Matrices
```{r}
# Using scores from Part A:

# TODO: Access the single value in row 1, column 2 using scores[1, 2]

scores[1, 2]
```

```{r}
# TODO: Access the entire first row using scores[1, ]

scores[1, ]
```

```{r}
# TODO: Access the entire "Ben" column using scores[, "Ben"]

scores[, "Ben"]
```

```{r}
# TODO: Return only the values in scores that are greater than or equal
# to 90 (hint: scores[scores >= 90] -- note the result loses its shape)

scores[scores >= 90]
```

Question #3

scores[1, ] and scores[, "Ben"] both return a result, but one represents a row and the other a column.
Run class() on each result. What data structure does R “downgrade” a single row/column of a matrix to, and why do you think R does this automatically?
```{r}
class(scores[1, ])
class(scores[, "Ben"])
```

Both of the result are numeric. Vector is the data structure that R "downgrade" a single row/column of a matrix to and R does this automatically because a single row or column only has one dimension and a vector is the simplest structure for it.

Question #4

In the matrix-logical chunk, the row/column names disappeared from your result. * Why does subsetting with a logical condition (scores >= 90) lose the 2D shape and names that scores[1, ] kept?

Subsetting with a logical condition (scores >= 90) lose the 2D shape and names that scores[1, ] kept because it only returns the values that meet the condition as a vector and dropping the rows or columns.

```{r}
scores_t
dim(scores_t)
```

```{r}
a + b
```

```{r}
a %*% b
```

Question #5

a * b and a %*% b both “multiply” the same two matrices but give different results.
Explain the difference between element-wise multiplication and matrix multiplication in your own words.

Element-wise multiplication multiplies the elements that have the same position in each matrix while matrix multiplication multiplies the elements in the row of a matrix to the elements in the column of another matrix and adds their product.

Question #6

t(scores) swaps rows and columns. Look at dim(scores) versus dim(scores_t).
Why must the row/column names also swap positions when you transpose a matrix?

The row/column names must also swap positions when transposing a matrix so that the labels will match the new positions of the elements that they represent.

### Part D - cbind() and rbind()
```{r}
# TODO: A new student "Dex" scored 85 on Quiz1 and 91 on Quiz2.
# Use cbind() to add a new column to scores called Dex with
# these two values. Store the result as scores_v2 and print it.

scores_v2 <- cbind(scores, Dex = c(85, 91))
scores_v2
```

```{r}
# TODO: A new quiz "Quiz3" was given with scores 80, 88, 93 for
# Ana, Ben, Cid (use only the original 3 students, not Dex).
# Use rbind() to add this as a new row to scores. Store as scores_v3
# and print it.

scores_v3 <- rbind(scores, Quiz3 = c(80, 88, 93))
scores_v3
```

Question #7 
What would happen if you tried cbind(scores, c(85, 91, 100)) — giving 3 values for a matrix that only has 2 rows? Test it, read the warning/error, and explain why cbind() and rbind()) require matching dimensions.
```{r}
cbind(scores, c(85, 91, 100))
```

The warning message shows: Warning in cbind(scores, c(85, 91, 100)): number of rows of result is not a
multiple of vector length (arg 2). The cbind() needs the same number of rows and the rbind() needs the same number of columns because the values have to line up correctly when combining matrices and to avoid warning or recycling of values.

Question #8

In what situation would you use rbind() instead of cbind() when updating a dataset over time?
Give a concrete example (e.g., daily sales, weekly attendance) and explain your reasoning.

I would use rbind() instead of cbind() to add new observations to a dataset over time. For example, if I record my daily study hours from Wednesday to Thursday, I can use rbind() to add my study hours for Friday as a new row because each day is a different observation while the columns remain unchanged.

```{r}
arr
```

```{r}
arr[1, 2, 2]
```

```{r}

arr[ , , 1]
```

```{r}
# TODO: Use dim() on arr to confirm its dimensions

dim(arr)
```

Question #9

A matrix needs 2 indices (scores[row, col]) but an array needs 3 (arr[row, col, layer]).
Using dim(arr), explain in your own words what each of the three numbers represents.

```{r}
dim(arr)
```

Using dim(arr) gives a result of 2 3 2. The leftmost 2 represents the number of rows, the 3 in the middle represents the number of columns and the rightmost 2 represents the number of layers.

Question #10

Give a real-world example of data that would naturally fit a 3D array structure (hint: think of something that has rows, columns, AND a third repeating dimension like time, subjects, or categories).

Explain why a single 2D matrix would not be enough.

For example, students test scores in first and second semester. The rows represent students, the columns represent subjects, and the third dimension represent the two different semesters. A single 2D matrix would not be enough because it can only store rows and columns for one semester at a time, while a 3D array can store the same students and subjects across multiple semesters in separate layers.

### Part F - Critical Thinking Challenge
```{r}
class_a <- matrix(c(85, 90, 78, 92), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                   dimnames = list(c("S1", "S2"), c("Midterm", "Final")))
class_b <- matrix(c(88, 84, 95, 91), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                   dimnames = list(c("S3", "S4"), c("Midterm", "Final")))

# TODO: Combine class_a and class_b into one matrix called all_students
# using the correct bind function (think about whether these represent
# new STUDENTS or new SCORE COLUMNS before choosing cbind or rbind)

all_students <- rbind(class_a, class_b)
all_students
```

```{r}
# TODO: From all_students, compute each student's average score across
# Midterm and Final. Hint: rowMeans(all_students) does this in one line.

rowMeans(all_students)
```

Question #11

Explain WHY you chose cbind() or rbind() in challenge-1.
What clue in the data (shared row names vs. shared column names) told you which function was correct?

I chose rbind() because class_a and class_b represent students. The clue in the data that told me the function rbind() was correct is that the two matrix have the same column names Midterm and Final but different row names from S1 to S4.

Question #12

Suppose instead of 2 classes you had 5 classes, each recorded as a separate matrix with the same 2 columns (Midterm, Final). Describe, in plain language (no code required), how you would combine all 5 into a single matrix, and how you would check your final result is correct using dim().

I would create a single matrix called all_students and store the result of the rbind() of the five separate matrices in it. Then, I would use dim() on the all_students matrix to check that all the students were combined correctly and that the number of columns stayed the same.

# Conclusion
In 3–4 sentences, summarize the key differences between a matrix and an array, and describe a situation where cbind()/rbind() would be useful in a real dataset you might work with.

A matrix is a 2D data structure with rows and columns, while an array can have two or more dimensions. Both of them are used to organize data, but arrays can handle more complex data. In a class record of quiz scores, I can use cbind() to add a new column for every quiz given by a teacher and I can use rbind() to add a new row when a new student joins the class.
